children: An analysis of how private bank stocks have performed under their respective CEOs suggests a clear trend. The biggest stock-market rewards have gone to CEOs who made fundamental changes in the banks, including bettering the asset quality, rather than those who took up the baton in banks perceived as stable ships.

That is the broad pattern emerging from a comparison of bank stocks from the start of the tenures of their current CEOs to August 31, 2026. Among the bigger banks ICICI Bank is the biggest standout at about 21 percent CAGR under Sandeep Bakhshi, followed by Axis Bank at 9.8 percent under Amitabh Chaudhry and IDFC First Bank at 9.3 percent under V Vaidyanathan.

By contrast, HDFC Bank has delivered a CAGR of just 2.6 percent under Sashidhar Jagdishan, while Kotak Mahindra Bank has risen 3.5 percent under Ashok Vaswani and CSB Bank has posted a negative CAGR of about 4 percent under Pralay Mondal.

RBL Bank is the top performers, with its stock rising 345 percent during R Subramaniakumar’s tenure, translating into a CAGR of around 45 percent. The stock’s strong gains over the past year have added to its outperformance, although the recent rally has also coincided with a major change in ownership with Emirates NBD emerging as a controlling shareholder, which has contributed to the re-rating.
Returns are split-adjusted share-price gains from each CEO’s start date to August 31, 2026, dividends are not included.
In short, numbers suggest that when a CEO has had to change the total look and feel of a bank, the eventual re-rating can be much larger.
This analysis excludes Yes Bank, Bandhan Bank, IndusInd Bank and Federal Bank, where the incumbent CEOs are yet to complete a full three-year term.
Sandeep Bakhshi: from repair to re-rating

Bakhshi took over ICICI Bank after one of the most difficult leadership episodes in Indian banking history. He succeeded Chanda Kochhar as MD & CEO on October 15, 2018, amid the fallout from the massive controversy surrounding her exit.
The numbers showed why the market was wary.

At September 2018, ICICI Bank’s net NPA ratio was 3.65 percent, even after falling from 4.19 percent in the previous quarter, while the bank added Rs 3,117 crore of gross NPAs in just the September quarter. Its provision coverage ratio was only 69.4 percent, according to company disclosures. The full-year FY18 picture was hardly comfortable either, with provisions having just reached Rs 17,307 crore, against profit after tax of Rs 6,777 crore.

The first phase of Bakhshi’s tenure was therefore less about chasing growth and more about repairing the franchise and rebuilding credibility. The market did not immediately reward him. ICICI’s stock ended 2019 at about Rs 539, after starting Bakhshi’s tenure at roughly Rs 321, and the COVID-19 shock subsequently drove it sharply lower in 2020.
The real re-rating came later, as asset quality improved and profitability strengthened.
By FY26, ICICI’ Bank's RoA had risen to 2.32 percent, up 90 basis points from FY21, while its gross NPA ratio had fallen to 1.4 percent.

By the time Bakhshi was reappointed for a second term in October 2023, the turnaround was already visible in the numbers. ICICI Bank’s gross NPA had fallen to 2.81 percent in March 2023 from the elevated levels of his early tenure, while net NPA stood at just 0.48 percent. FY23 profit had surged to Rs 31,896 crore, up from Rs 6,777 crore in FY18.
The stock has risen about 66 percent from its March 2023 level to August 31, 2026, adding to the gains delivered through the earlier phase of the turnaround.
Vaidyanathan: Changed the business
IDFC First Bank is a similar example.

V Vaidyanathan took charge in December 2018 after the merger of IDFC Bank and Capital First. His central proposition was to transform a largely wholesale-oriented bank into a retail-focused lender. He publicly set out an ambition of eventually moving towards a 70:30 retail-wholesale mix, arguing that retail loans offered better yields and more predictable credit quality.

The bank has gradually reduced the legacy infrastructure and wholesale book while building retail businesses. Its gross NPA ratio has fallen from 3.7 percent in March 2022 to 1.6 percent in March 2026, while the legacy wholesale portfolio’s GNPA has fallen from 7.2 percent to 2.2 percent, according to company disclosures.
The stock has doubled over Vaidyanathan’s tenure. That makes IDFC First another case where the CEO was not merely managing an established franchise but changing what the franchise was.
Amitabh Chaudhry: Turnaround at Axis Bank

Amitabh Chaudhry’s Axis Bank story also fits the pattern. He took charge in January 2019 when asset quality was a major investor concern. The bank’s gross NPA ratio was 6.52 percent in FY19, with RoA at only 0.40 percent, according to company disclosures.

Under Chaudhry, the bank spent years cleaning up the balance sheet, strengthening provisions and rebuilding profitability. By FY21, gross NPA had fallen to 3.70 percent and RoA had recovered to 0.70 percent.

By FY26, Axis’s RoA had reached 1.46 percent, while gross NPA was down to 1.23 percent. The stock has gained about 107 percent since Chaudhry took charge, translating into a CAGR of roughly 9.8 percent.
CSB: Market Yet to Buy Growth Story
CSB Bank is where the narrative becomes more nuanced.

Pralay Mondal took over in September 2022, but he did not inherit a bank that needed the same kind of massive overhaul. Much of the clean-up and repositioning had already taken place before he took over and his task was clear: to take the bank to the next level, and deliver growth without sacrificing the gains already made.
That has produced mixed results.

CSB’s advances grew 26 percent year-on-year to Rs 39,848 crore in FY26, while deposits rose 20 percent. Its RoA, however, fell to 1.26 percent from 1.49 percent in FY25, even as gross NPA remained relatively contained at 1.66 percent, according to company disclosures.

Mondal himself has outlined ambitions for faster growth, including 25 percent or more asset growth. Yet the stock has fallen about 15 percent since he took charge, implying a negative CAGR of roughly 4 percent. That stands in sharp contrast to the gains delivered by the CEOs who inherited banks in need of a more visible reset.
The challenge, then, is different from Bakhshi’s. There was no broken story to repair. The task was to create the next growth story. So far, the market has yet to fully buy it.
HDFC and Kotak: No major Re-rating

Jagdishan inherited HDFC Bank from Aditya Puri, who had already built one of India’s strongest banking franchises. His tenure was dominated by the massive merger with HDFC Ltd and the subsequent task of integrating the combined institution. Operationally, the bank remains strong. RoA was around 1.96 percent in FY26, even as NIMs compressed, according to the company's investor presentations.

But the stock has delivered only a modest gain since Jagdishan took charge, part of which is due to the ongoing leadership crisis in the bank, particularly since March this year when the previous chairman, Atanu Chakraborthy, abruptly resigned, sparking governance-related concerns which are ongoing.

Ashok Vaswani's case is also somewhat similarly as he inherited Kotak Bank from a position of strength. Among the bankers considered, his would be the shortest tenure of three years, which is set to end in December 2026, Kotak Mahindra Bank stock’s near 10 percent gain is something of an underperformance when seen against re-rating enjoyed by ICICI, Axis or IDFC First.

title: ICICI Bank tops the chart under Sandeep Bakhshi's leadership
